title: What abuse prevention training must disability welfare service providers in Japan run?
description: Japan's disability welfare abuse prevention duties: committee, annual staff training, officer, restraint training, 2022 commencement and 2024 fee cuts.
shortAnswer: Since April 1, 2022, every designated disability welfare service provider in Japan must hold an abuse prevention committee, train staff in abuse prevention periodically and appoint an officer in charge, under Article 40-2 of MHLW Ordinance No. 171 of 2006 and the Disability Abuse Prevention Act. MHLW guidance expects training at least once a year and at every hire, with records. Since April 2024, missing measures trigger a 1% fee reduction.
keyTakeaways: Article 15 of the Act on the Prevention of Abuse of Persons with Disabilities (Act No. 79 of 2011) requires disability facilities and service operators to take abuse prevention measures, naming staff training and a complaints system.

Article 40-2 of the disability services standards (MHLW Ordinance No. 171 of 2006) sets three concrete measures: a periodic abuse prevention committee, periodic staff training and a designated officer. They were effort obligations until March 31, 2022 under MHLW Ordinance No. 10 of 2021.
MHLW's interpretive notice expects abuse prevention training at least once a year, always at hiring, recorded in writing, and committee records kept for five years.
A parallel duty on physical restraint (Article 35-2(3)) requires a committee, a guideline and training on appropriate use of restraint, also at least once a year and at hiring.
The fiscal 2024 fee revision introduced a 1% reduction for providers missing any abuse prevention measure and raised the restraint reduction to 10% for facility and residential services.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) Department of Health and Welfare for Persons with Disabilities, with prefectures and municipalities as designating and inspecting authorities
appliesTo: Designated disability welfare service providers under the Act on Comprehensive Support for Persons with Disabilities, such as home care, daily life care, employment support and group homes
Designated disability support facilities, under the parallel facility standards
All service staff and managers, including part-time staff
Abuse prevention officers and abuse prevention committee members

sections.heading: Which laws require abuse prevention training in disability services?

blocks.text: Two layers apply. The statutory layer is the **Act on the Prevention of Abuse of Persons with Disabilities and Support for Caregivers** (障害者虐待防止法, Act No. 79 of 2011). Article 15 requires founders of disability welfare facilities and operators of disability welfare service businesses to take measures to prevent abuse by their staff, including "the implementation of training" for staff and a system for handling complaints from users and families ([Disability Abuse Prevention Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/423AC1000000079)).

The operational layer is the designation standards. The **Standards for Personnel, Equipment and Operation of Designated Disability Welfare Services** (指定障害福祉サービスの事業等の人員、設備及び運営に関する基準, MHLW Ordinance No. 171 of 2006), made under the Act on Comprehensive Support for the Daily and Social Lives of Persons with Disabilities, turn the general duty into specific measures. Article 3(3) states the principle that every provider must build the systems needed to protect users' human rights and prevent abuse, and must train its staff. Article 40-2 then sets the measures ([disability services standards, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/418M60000100171)).

Article 40-2 is written for home care (kyotaku kaigo) and applied to most other services through cross-reference articles. Designated disability support facilities have a parallel Article 54-2 in their own standards ordinance, and standards for disabled children's services carry similar provisions.
Article 40-2 requires providers, to prevent abuse and its recurrence, to take three measures:

items: hold an abuse prevention committee periodically (video conferencing is allowed) and make sure staff are fully informed of its results;
run abuse prevention training for staff periodically; and
appoint a person in charge of implementing the first two measures.

blocks.text: Unlike the parallel long-term care standard, Article 40-2 does not itself require a written abuse prevention guideline. MHLW's interpretive notice says providers should preferably prepare one, covering the basic approach, the committee, the training policy, reporting methods, response when abuse occurs and how users can view the guideline. Where a guideline exists, training should apply it.

MHLW Ordinance No. 10 of 2021 inserted these measures from April 1, 2021, but its supplementary provisions (Article 2) treated them as effort obligations until March 31, 2022. They have been binding since April 1, 2022, and as at November 2026 no further transitional relief applies to them.

sections.heading: How often must abuse prevention training run, and what should it cover?

blocks.text: MHLW expects at least one session a year plus training at every hire. The interpretive notice on the disability services standards (障発第1206001号, as revised) says training should spread basic knowledge of abuse prevention and, where the provider has a guideline, apply it. To make staff education stick, the provider should run a training program prepared by its abuse prevention committee, "periodically (at least once a year)", and "always" run abuse prevention training at hiring. The content delivered must be recorded ([MHLW interpretive notice comparison table](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001494357.pdf)).

The notice allows flexibility in delivery. Training inside the organization counts, and so does attendance at training run by a regional self-support council (jiritsu shien kyōgikai) or a core consultation support center. It also says the officer in charge and the manager should preferably attend the abuse prevention training run by prefectures under the community life support program.

The committee is framed as a learning system rather than a disciplinary one. The notice says it is not intended to punish staff, and describes a cycle in which incidents and inappropriate care are reported on a standard form, collected and analyzed, causes and recurrence measures are worked out, results are shared with staff and the effect of measures is checked. Committee activity must be recorded and the records kept for five years.

sections.heading: What training applies to physical restraint?

blocks.text: Physical restraint has its own duty, closely linked to abuse prevention. Article 35-2 prohibits physical restraint and other restriction of a user's movement except where urgently unavoidable to protect the life or body of the user or others, requires any restraint to be recorded with its method, duration, the user's condition and the reason, and, in paragraph 3, requires three measures: a periodic committee on appropriate use of restraint, a written guideline, and periodic staff training. The restraint measures also became binding on April 1, 2022 under Article 5 of the 2021 supplementary provisions.

The interpretive notice sets the same training rhythm: a program based on the guideline, run periodically at least once a year, and always at hiring, with records. It notes that restraint training can be run together with other training, such as abuse prevention training, provided restraint is covered.

sections.heading: What happens if a provider does not comply?

blocks.text: Since the fiscal 2024 disability welfare fee revision, gaps reduce monthly income. MHLW's summary of the main revisions lists a new **reduction for not implementing abuse prevention measures** of 1% of the prescribed units, applied to providers that have not held the committee, run periodic training or appointed the officer. The same revision raised the **reduction for not implementing restraint elimination measures** from 5 units to 10% of prescribed units for facility and residential services (disability support facilities, medical-type care, group homes and others) and set it at 1% for visiting and day services ([MHLW fiscal 2024 disability fee revision, main points](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001216034.pdf)).

Under Article 16 of the Disability Abuse Prevention Act, anyone who discovers a person with a disability who appears to have been abused by facility staff must report it promptly to the municipality, and staff may not be dismissed or otherwise disadvantaged for reporting. Under Article 20, prefectural governors publish each fiscal year the state of abuse by facility staff and the measures taken. Compliance with the standards is checked by the designating prefecture or municipality, because meeting them is a condition of keeping the designation.

sections.heading: Which other training duties apply to disability services?

blocks.text: The same 2021 ordinance introduced business continuity planning (Article 33-2) and infection prevention measures (Article 34(3)) for disability services, each with periodic staff training and drills. Those duties had a longer grace period and became binding on April 1, 2024, the same date as for long-term care providers. The pattern mirrors the [April 2024 long-term care mandates](/regulations/japan-long-term-care-mandatory-training-2024), though frequencies in the disability notice differ by service. Employers of persons with disabilities outside the welfare system have a separate duty under Article 21 of the Abuse Prevention Act to train workers and handle complaints, and broader workplace obligations are covered in [Japan's disability reasonable accommodation obligations](/regulations/japan-disability-reasonable-accommodation-obligations).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats Article 15 of the Act, Articles 35-2 and 40-2 of the standards and the interpretive notice as linked obligations, and connects them to the provider's own guideline and committee findings. Learning outcomes and assessment points are defined before content, so new committee findings can be traced into the next training cycle.

faqs.q: Is a written abuse prevention guideline mandatory for disability service providers?
faqs.a: Not under Article 40-2 itself, which requires a committee, training and an officer. MHLW's interpretive notice says providers should preferably prepare a guideline and lists the items it should cover. For physical restraint, by contrast, Article 35-2(3) does require a written guideline.

faqs.q: Can staff attend external training instead of in-house sessions?
faqs.a: Yes. MHLW's interpretive notice accepts training run inside the organization and attendance at training run by a regional self-support council or a core consultation support center. The provider should keep a record of who attended which session and what it covered.

faqs.q: When did abuse prevention measures become mandatory for disability services?
faqs.a: April 1, 2022. MHLW Ordinance No. 10 of 2021 added the measures from April 1, 2021 but treated them as effort obligations for one year. Business continuity planning and infection prevention measures had a three-year grace period and became binding on April 1, 2024.

faqs.q: How large is the fee reduction for missing abuse prevention measures?
faqs.a: One percent of the prescribed units, introduced in the fiscal 2024 disability welfare fee revision. It applies where any required abuse prevention measure is missing: the committee, periodic training or the designated officer. The separate restraint reduction is 10% for facility and residential services and 1% for visiting and day services.
